4649.heavy: Not a conditioning factor for position: the source states weight is the CORRELATE of stress ('el correlato del acento es el peso prosódico'; 'la sílaba prominente debe ser pesada'), i.e. the stressed syllable must be bimoraic (long vowel in an open syllable, or a moraic fortis-consonant coda); first members of compounds lose their mora by position (p. 145-146).
4649.prule: final (right edge of the phonological word): the lexicon is mostly monosyllabic; in the disyllabic words that exist (root-root compounds, Spanish loans) prominence falls on the last syllable, which is the bimoraic 'well-formed foot', while the first syllable is reduced to a monomoraic 'ill-formed foot' — an iambic light-heavy (CVµ CVµµ) pattern

4650.dloc: Rastorgueva 1999, p. 167, article 'Сангесари язык//диалект', section 'Фонологические сведения', paragraph immediately after the consonant table (begins 'Ударение у именных частей речи').
4650.prule: Fixed final stress in the nominal parts of speech, 'as a rule' (как правило) on the last syllable of the word: dasté 'handle', mɛrkeyín 'man', kuté 'child'; stress-bearing suffixes added to the word take it (plural mɛrkeyinún, kåtún; comparative γašangtár). Outside the stress domain: the oblique-case ending -i (Hasáni kɛtåb 'Hasan's book', kåtúni kɛtåb 'the children's book'), the indefinite article -i (mɛrkeyín-i boya 'there was a man') and the postpositions dɛ, re, mu. Syllable weight is never mentioned. Christensen 1935 agrees by reference (§ 29: same rules as Sourkhéï/Läsguerdī, which § 35 says 'suivent en général les mêmes règles que le persan') and in his paradigms § 111 (pøsé, pəsé, pøsér / pøséri / pøsérde; œsbé / œsbéi / œsbéde; žení / ženúni / ženúnde; kʰotún / kʰotúni / kʰotúnde: accent on the last syllable of the stem or of the plural suffix, oblique -i and accusative -de unaccented).
4650.srule: No secondary stress is described by Rastorgueva 1999. Christensen 1935 § 29 notes only that in negated verb forms the negative prefix carries the main accent while 'un accent secondaire' may rest on the theme or the ending; no positional secondary rule is given. (The verb facts formerly filed here are primary-stress rules: past tense on the last stem syllable, present on the ending, negative forms on the negation prefix - see prule/quote.)

4651.heavy: Not framed as weight: syllables whose vowel is anything other than the high central ɨ take stress in the default position; a syllable whose vowel is ɨ is 'normally' skipped ('unless the vowel in those syllables is the high central ɨ'; 'normally excepting those syllables with ɨ'), and the paragoge -ɨq is never stressed. Sneddon writes the same vowel as ə.
4651.dflt: Maryott p. 268: 'in words where there is no vowel but ɨ... the placement of stress is quite unpredictable' (his p. 272 examples ma'kɨgɨng 'dried' vs malɨ'gɨng 'sad'); Scheller 1991 p. 7: 'This author has yet to find an example of a word whose only vowel is /ɨ/ that has stress other than on the penult.'
4651.prule: Primary stress (realised as stress plus high pitch) falls on the penultimate syllable of the word; the paragoge -ɨq is skipped, so words ending in it are stressed on the antepenult (the base's penult); a syllable whose vowel is the high central ɨ (barred i, schwa-like) is normally skipped and stress moves rightward ('in the progressive direction') onto the final syllable (tɨ'aq 'fly'; Sneddon: 'except if this contains ə and the final syllable contains some other vowel, in which case stress falls on the final syllable'). Words whose only vowel is ɨ are 'quite unpredictable' (Maryott; Scheller finds only penult). Stated as holding 'in the majority of words'; a 'small class of stems' has contrastive, phonologically unpredictable stress.
4651.srule: In words of more than three syllables a secondary stress falls on the third or the fourth syllable before the primary-stressed syllable: /ˌka.la.lɨn.ˈsuŋ/ 's.t. carried on the head', /ˌmɨ.pa.pɨ.ˈri.no/ 'to make correct', /qi.ˌpɨ.pɨ.bi.ˈsa.la/ 'to converse' (third before); /ˌma.ka.pa.mɨ.ˈɭi/ 'to be able to buy', /ˌka.ta.ti.ki.ˈla.neŋ/ 'bed' (fourth before); which of the two occurs is 'not predictable' (Scheller 1991, own fieldwork). The primary source for the primary rule, Maryott 1977 p. 272, treats primary stress only, 'due to the need for further study of secondary stress'.

The system is very similar to the Bamako dialect except that high tones do not rise in pitch after low tones, but rather are manifested on the same pitch level. High tones only rise in pitch when there is a following low tone.... This rule is very similar to the readjustment of tone in Bambara dialects after the assignment of accent.' 4654.heavy: Heavy = syllable with a long vowel (two moras: 'la cantidad vocálica es contrastiva... tres patrones... ˈVV#, ˈV$V# y ˈVV$V#'). Codas do not count: 'Las únicas consonantes permitidas en la posición de coda son ’, y y w; ninguna es moraica' (p. 110). Length is itself licensed by stress: 'La cantidad vocálica está anclada por el acento' (p. 109); a long vowel that loses stress under suffixation is shortened with tone deletion (ICUWPL 2, p. 59).
4654.dflt: penultimate syllable (ˈV$V#); a monomoraic word with no preceding word in the phrase takes a stressed prothetic i- (%ˈi-CV#) to meet a bimoraic minimum
4654.prule: Stress falls on the syllable containing the penultimate mora of the word, counted from the right edge: the final syllable is stressed when its vowel is long (ˈVV#), otherwise the penultimate syllable (ˈV$V#, ˈVV$V#). Vowel length is contrastive (long vowel = two moras); the only codas (’, y, w) are non-moraic, so weight is vowel length alone. Equivalent formulation: final syllable if heavy (long vowel), else penult.

4655.prule: San Miguel el Grande proper (Pike 1947, first-hand, sec. 7.1): the lexical morpheme in its full form is a bisyllabic couplet (CVCV, CVʔCV, CVV, CVʔV, with or without final nasalization). Stress, when present, falls on the first syllable of the morpheme and never on its second syllable, so a heard stress marks a morpheme beginning; the stress is optional and often undetectable ('frequently I can detect no extra intensity on it whatever'). The site is defined on the morpheme, not on the phonological word: reduced monosyllabic proclitics and enclitics are morphemes in reduced form that attach to a full morpheme, and Pike says only that this reduction 'complicates' the indication of potential initial stress and that a stress mark 'at the beginning of every morpheme' would insist on 'a feature that is frequently absent'; his solution is orthographic (spaces and hyphens, fn. 34: hyphens for postclitics, spaces after proclitics). He does not say that clitics are stressless, and Dyk & Stoudt 1973: 118 say the enclitic, though part of the preceding word, 'conserva su propio acento'. Not computable from word syllable count; not weight-sensitive; no secondary stress and no one-stress-per-word (culminativity) statement.
4655.srule: Not mentioned in Pike 1947 (repr. Brend 1972, sec. 7-8, pp. 44-48 read): Pike describes only optional stress on the first syllable of the bisyllabic morpheme and says nothing about secondary or rhythmic stress; Dyk 1959: 221 and Dyk & Stoudt 1965: 118 (same variety) give none either.

4656.prule: Two contrastive, lexically assigned stress types, both confined to the last two syllables of the phonological word: consonant stress (about 75-80% of morphemes) lengthens a consonant of the ultima ('in nearly all words with consonant stress, the stress occurs on the ultima'; 2011: 'la consonante alargada siempre pertenece a la última sílaba'); vowel stress lengthens the vowel of the penult (2011: 'se acentúa la vocal de la penúltima sílaba'; 1977 'vowel stress moves to the penult' under suffixation, though its own transcriptions also show final-vowel stress in some words, e.g. nta²se·² 'coffee'). Which type a root carries is not predictable from its shape (minimal pairs 1977 p. 69: sa²k·o³ 'pineapple' vs sa·²¹ko² 'jacket'; ko²č·e² 'louse' vs ko²če·³ 'fish'), except that a vowel-initial final syllable takes vowel accent automatically (2011 p. 11: ni.o 'tortilla', na.a 'uno') and that consonant stress cannot sit on a syllable with a two-tone sequence.

4657.dq: Cada palabra tiene una sílaba que está acentuada, o sea, se pronuncia con una intensidad mayor que las otras sílabas de la palabra. Esta sílaba es generalmente la última de la raíz de la palabra y no se indica con un acento escrito.

4657.prule: Exactly one stressed syllable per word (greater intensity), located on the last syllable of the ROOT: prefixes before the root (qui-, to-, tsi-) and suffixes after it (-ha', -hin) are unstressed, so the stressed syllable is word-final in unsuffixed words (qui-tscu, to-tsi-nein, qui-so-jndëë) but non-final in suffixed ones (tachi-hö', toju'-hin). Stress is not written; position is set by morphological structure, not by syllable count or weight.
4657.srule: None: 'Cada palabra tiene una sílaba que está acentuada, o sea, se pronuncia con una intensidad mayor que las otras sílabas de la palabra' (one stressed syllable per word; no secondary or rhythmic stress mentioned in §0.3, pp. 371-373). tn.quote: Las silabas son de dos clases: balisticas y controladas. ... Hay ocho tonos: cuatro se presentan en sílabas balísticas y cuatro en sílabas controladas. Las letras de los tonos corresponden a niveles de tonalidad alto, medio y bajo y a dos deslices, uno para abajo y otro para arriba. Los tonos de las sílabas controladas tienden a levantarse ligeramente; los tonos de las sílabas balísticas tienden a un deslizamiento hacia abajo. ... Ejemplos: ndiaa (a) tela, ropa ndia (a-m) mi ropa tyee (m-m) sacerdote tye (m) papá jndéé (b-b) monte jndé (b) zacate chuee (m-a) huipil su (a-b) azul
tn.translation: Syllables are of two kinds: ballistic and controlled. ... There are eight tones: four occur in ballistic syllables and four in controlled syllables. The tone letters correspond to high, mid and low pitch levels and to two glides, one downward and one upward. The tones of controlled syllables tend to rise slightly; the tones of ballistic syllables tend to glide downward. ... Examples: ndiaa (a) cloth, clothes; ndia (a-m) my clothes; tyee (m-m) priest; tye (m) dad; jndéé (b-b) bush; jndé (b) grass; chuee (m-a) huipil; su (a-b) blue

4658.dq: Las palabras morfológicamente simples en la lengua las podemos dividir en monosílabos y bisílabos. ... Por su parte, los bisílabos presentan una sílaba átona y una sílaba tónica (Galván p. 77); obligatoriamente hay uno y solo un acento primario por palabra fonológica (Ocotitla Maciel p. 24).

4658.tone: Two lexical tones, high vs low, contrastive only in the stressed syllable and only in modal or first-mora-creaky syllables that are open or have a lenis coda (pp. 76-77); high is the default/unmarked tone; the unstressed syllable of a bisyllable always has mid pitch (p. 77). In connected texts tone often changes or disappears when two tonic syllables are adjacent (p. 80). A tone language with clear word-level stress, so coded by stress position, not TONAL.

tn.quote: El diidx zah cuenta únicamente con dos tonos léxicos; uno alto y uno bajo. ... el tono sólo contrasta en sílabas sin rasgo de fonación (modales) ... o en sílabas con el rasgo [+glotis constreñida] anclado únicamente a la primera mora ... Cabe especificar que el tono, al igual que el contraste fuerte-suave y la fonación contrastiva, sólo se presenta en sílaba tónica. ... la sílaba átona presenta siempre una tonía media y la sílaba tónica puede presentar un tono alto o un tono bajo. ... Proponer a la segunda mora como la Unidad Portadora de Tono (UPT) nos permite solucionar todos los fenómenos
tn.translation: Diidx zah has only two lexical tones; one high and one low. ... tone only contrasts in syllables without a phonation feature (modal) ... or in syllables with [+constricted glottis] anchored only to the first mora ... It should be specified that tone, like the fortis-lenis contrast and contrastive phonation, only occurs in the tonic syllable. ... the atonic syllable always has mid pitch and the tonic syllable may have a high or a low tone. ... Proposing the second mora as the Tone-Bearing Unit (TBU) lets us resolve all the phenomena

4660.dq: Por regla general el acento en las palabras huaves carga en la última sílaba.
4660.dloc: p. 27, section ACENTO (of the archive.org scan lenguasdelestad00belmgoog; header '—27—'; archive.org); p. 18
4660.heavy: A syllable with a full vowel can bear stress; a final syllable whose vowel is 'muda' (Belmar's ì with grave accent, 'semi-muda', which also gives the preceding consonant its strong sound, p. 18) cannot, and stress retreats to the penult: 'Si la palabra termina en vocal muda el acento carga en la penúltima sílaba.' Nothing is said about closed syllables or vowel length.
4660.dflt: unstated (Belmar gives no example or statement for a word whose last two syllables both have mute vowels; every example has a full vowel in the final or the penult)
4660.prule: Stress on the final syllable ('Por regla general el acento... carga en la última sílaba') unless the word ends in a 'mute vowel' (Belmar's grave-accented ì, defined on p. 18 as 'semi-muda' and as giving the preceding consonant its strong sound), in which case stress is on the penult. Belmar counts the mute vowel as a syllable ('penúltima sílaba'), so on the source's own terms the position depends on the full vs. reduced quality of the final vowel (rightmost full-vowel syllable, within a two-syllable right-edge window), not on syllable count alone.

4664.prule: Stress on the penultimate syllable of the word. van Hoëvell 1877 states it for the Ambonese land language (all five dialects incl. Saparua): 'in den regel valt op de voorlaatste lettergreep', naming only Haruku and Asilulu as erratic (pp. 13-14; p. 11 calls penult 'den algemeenen regel'). Stresemann 1927 § 177 derives it from the Ur-Ambon penult and every accented Saparua ('Spr.') form he cites is surface-penult after the suffix-vowel loss (látu-l, húwa-l, muláha-l, utó'-o-l, ulát-o-l, nuwól-lo, után-no, urít-i-l, palá-e, tomá-lo). Suffixes: verbal -e and (as a rule) verbal -lo move the accent to the new penult; the nominal ending -lo does not count for the accent, but its vowel is 'meist verstummt' in Saparua so the surface word is again penult-stressed; where the vowel survives (háu-lo, móti-lo) the stress sits on the stem penult = surface antepenult; usál-lo (< usáli) is surface-penult (see the exceptions block).

4669.prule: Stress falls on the lexical root. In the canonical sesquisyllabic prefix+root word the prefix (first syllable) is unstressed, short and reduced to Ciə-/Ci- (yielding the apparent onset clusters) and the root (second syllable) is stressed and longer; Bodt labels this 'iambic' and phrases it positionally ('stressing the second syllable of a word') but immediately qualifies it as 'always the root and not the prefix' (2024 p. 170). Grammatical suffixes (case markers incl. the locative, the plural marker, the imperative suffix) are unstressed in all varieties (2024 §50c p. 301: short -ɔˀ reflexes in Khoina, Jerigaon, Khoitam, Rahung 'conditioned by a lack of stress on these suffixes'; plural-marker entry: 'always found as an unstressed bound suffix'), so in root+suffix words the stressed syllable is the root, i.e. word-initial. The invariant across Bodt's statements is root stressed / affixes unstressed, not a counted syllable position. One sentence in Bodt's 2018 working note (p. 2) says the opposite for root+suffix bisyllables ('a suffix preceded by an unstressed root'); the same note states two pages later that 'the root always carried the stress, a situation that is reflected in the comtemporary Sartang and Sherdukpen varieties' (p. 4), marks stress on the root in every Sartang form it transcribes, and is superseded on this point by the 2024 monograph of record.
4669.srule: Not mentioned in Bodt 2024 (Ch. IV secs. 4.1-4.4.1 pp. 155-172, Ch. VI sec. 50b-50c pp. 300-301, plural-marker entry) or in Bodt 2018 (Zenodo 1284482, 5 pp.): neither says anything about secondary or rhythmic stress in Sartang.

4669.tone: No tone system described for Sartang. Each Sartang variety contrasts long modal/breathy vowels with short glottal-constricted, creaky vowels carrying rising pitch, treated by Bodt as a vowel contrast, not lexical tone: sec. 3.5 Khoitam p. 101: 'Khoitam makes a distinction between long, modal or breathy voiced vowels /e, ɛ, i, ɔ, u/ and short, creaky, glottal constricted vowel variants with rising pitch /eˀ, ɛˀ, iˀ, ɔˀ, uˀ/.'; sec. 3.6 Rahung p. 118: 'Like Khoitam, Rahung makes a distinction between long, modal, or breathy vowels /e, ɛ, i, o, ɔ, u/ and short, creaky, glottal constricted vowels with rising pitch /eˀ, ɛˀ, iˀ, oˀ, ɔˀ, uˀ/.' (Bodt's one 'rising tone vowel phoneme uq' remark, sec. 3.1.1 Duhumbi vowels p. 59, concerns a single Duhumbi lexeme, not Sartang.) Bodt 2018 p. 2 heading 'Constricted syllables always unstressed' ties the short constricted rhymes to unstressed position (there for Duhumbi; 2024 §50c applies the same conditioning to the Sartang suffix reflexes). The acute accents in Bodt's Sartang Lexicon word lists mark that vowel series on monosyllables, not stress.

4671.prule: Word stress ('accento d'intensità sillabica' = 'accento di parola') is fixed per lexical item and contrastive (farà /faˈra/ 'to go down' vs fara /ˈfara/ '(s)he goes down'); no phonological predictor is given. The orthography leaves penultimate stress unmarked as the default, and the source's own examples show final stress (all infinitives farà, abé, finí; caffè, però, aió, parchí, piú), antepenultimate stress (fèmmina, pazènzia, pégura, sciòbaru, àgliu, faràbami) and fourth-from-last stress (tinàgliuru, fazarísthiani). dfl.note: The source gives no count, but treats penultimate stress as the unmarked default: its minimal-accent rule writes the stress mark on final, antepenultimate and fourth-from-last stressed words and never on penultimate-stressed ones, on the stated principle that graphic accents should mark only the rare cases; the default is thus orthographic/implicit, not a stated phonological rule.
dfl.q: Se si vuole indicare quali siano le sillabe intense delle parole usando il minor numero di accenti grafici, si può adottare la regola che prevede di accentare graficamente, oltre alle vocali ultime, anche le terzultime e le quartultime, ma non le penultime ... Le lingue che utilizzano l’accento grafico tendono infatti a segnalare solo quelli rari
dfl.c: Marras, Mura & Virdis 2022, Standard ortografico della lingua turritana o sassarese

vlen.q: Il fonema vibrante sonoro scempio /r/ dopo vocale o consonante ha una realizzazione lenita, caratterizzata da un solo momento di contatto tra la punta della lingua e gli alveoli: mari /ˈmari/ [ˈmaːɾi], sirenu /siˈrɛnu/ [siˈɾɛːnu].
vlen.c: Marras, Mura & Virdis 2022, Standard ortografico della lingua turritana o sassarese
